text:
Thanks. I found Q3 surprisingly difficult – balancing privacy with potential help feels really fraught. Specifically, deciding on ‘small’, ‘moderate’ or ‘large’ improvements felt arbitrary without knowing *how* that translates to real students being helped.

I think questions around fairness (Q5) are most vital; a biased system could be actively harmful. Also, the explainability trade-offs (Q4) – we need to understand *why* someone is flagged.

My answers on nationality and financial aid differed slightly from the majority wanting even minimal improvement. As an international student who works part-time, I'm wary of those being used against me, however subtly. Perhaps a clear opt-out would ease concerns there, separate from model design?

Thanks. I agree with S2 about Q3 being difficult – quantifying ‘improvement’ feels artificial when we're talking about students’ lives. It's hard to weigh potential benefits against privacy risks without more context on *how* the data will be secured and used.

I think Q4, explainability, is absolutely crucial from an advisor’s perspective. We need to be able to discuss flags with students meaningfully – “the model says…” isn't helpful if we can’t elaborate. 

My answers were fairly aligned with the group overall, though I leaned towards ‘moderate’ on Absalon data (Q3.4) as consistent engagement *can* signal struggles, but only alongside other factors. The strong consensus against using age, gender or ethnicity is reassuring; those feel like red lines, and an opt-out, as S2 suggested, feels vital for things like financial aid where vulnerabilities are clear.

Thanks both of you. I agree with S2 and A3 that quantifying “improvement” in Q3 felt really difficult – it’s hard to put a number on helping someone. The lack of context makes it feel a bit… abstract.

For me, the explainability questions (Q4) were *the* most important. As someone with dyslexia, I'm already aware of how systems can unintentionally disadvantage certain groups. If a model flags me but no one can clearly explain why, it feels like another barrier, not support. 

I was stricter on data use than the majority, especially regarding nationality and financial aid – those feel too easily misused. Opt-outs are good, but better data security protocols from the start would be ideal, and transparency about how data is stored.

Thanks to S2, A3 and S7 for raising those points – I completely agree with much of it. Q3 *was* hard; defining ‘improvement’ feels detached from the individual student. And yes, a clear understanding of data security is paramount before even considering adding more data sources.

I think Q5, fairness, resonated most strongly with me because of my own experience restarting my studies here after dropping out elsewhere. A system needs to be equitable – actively working *against* bias, not just avoiding it.

My stricter stance on nationality and financial aid comes from being an EU student who had to navigate a new system while also working. Those factors can feel…stigmatizing. An opt-out is good, but transparency about how data is used would be even better – maybe regular audits?

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what's been said - Q3 *was* tough. As an advisor for eleven years, quantifying ‘improvement’ feels distant from the individual students I work with. We’re talking about people, not just data points.

I think explainability – Q4 – is absolutely critical. My colleagues and I spend a lot of time building rapport with students; a black-box model undermines that trust. 

I landed on ‘small’ for Absalon data (Q3.4) because *patterns* can be informative, but only in context. And like others, I'm very hesitant about nationality or financial aid - an opt-out is a good start, but robust security and transparency are essential to avoid unintended consequences. The focus needs to be on proactively supporting students, not labelling them.

Thanks everyone. I agree with a lot of what’s been said – Q3 *was* difficult. As an international student just starting my master's here, quantifying “improvement” feels really abstract when it impacts real people trying to adjust.

For me, the questions around explainability (Q4) are most important. Coming from a different educational system, I want to understand *why* any flags arise – it’s about trust and feeling supported, not judged by an opaque system. 

I was stricter on data use regarding nationality. It feels sensitive as a newcomer adapting to everything here. While an opt-out is good, transparent security practices are vital. Regular audits sound like a positive step too, showing accountability.

Thanks everyone, I agree with much of what’s been said – Q3 *was* particularly difficult to answer; trying to quantify ‘improvement’ feels… detached from real lives. As someone managing a long-term condition alongside my thesis, I'm acutely aware of how easily systems can unintentionally disadvantage students.

For me, explainability (Q4) is critical. Understanding *why* a flag appears helps me advocate for myself and access the right support. The questions around fairness (Q5) also resonated deeply – equity is essential. 

I was stricter on sensitive data like nationality & disability, reflecting my own concerns about potential bias. While opt-outs are good, transparency in data handling *and* clear appeals processes feel vital to build trust.

Thanks everyone. I wholeheartedly agree with S9 and others about Q3 feeling incredibly difficult – quantifying ‘improvement’ feels… wrong when we're talking about students struggling. It lacks nuance.

For me, explainability (Q4) is *crucial*. As someone managing a chronic health condition impacting my studies, being able to understand *why* I might be flagged allows me to advocate for myself and demonstrate context the model wouldn’t know. 

My stricter answers regarding disability data stem from personal experience with navigating support services – it needs careful handling. While an opt-out is welcome, truly robust security and transparent data usage are paramount. A clear appeals process would also provide vital reassurance.

Thanks everyone. I definitely agree with a lot of what’s been said about Q3 being difficult – trying to put numbers on ‘improvement’ feels really weird when we're talking about supporting people. It felt abstract and disconnected.

I think explainability (Q4) is massively important, especially given my experiences restarting here after dropping out. Knowing *why* I was flagged would help me understand if it's a genuine issue or just something the model doesn’t ‘get’. 

My stricter stance on things like nationality and financial aid comes from that experience – feeling vulnerable and judged. An opt-out is good, but real transparency about how this data is handled is vital to rebuild trust and ensure fairness for everyone.

Thanks everyone, it’s really helpful hearing all these perspectives. I agree wholeheartedly with S2, A3 and others that Q3 was incredibly difficult; quantifying ‘improvement’ felt very disconnected from real student experiences. As someone who dropped out of a previous programme, I know how easily things can derail. 

For me, explainability – Q4 – is vital. Knowing *why* the model flags someone allows for constructive conversations and targeted support. I was stricter on nationality and financial aid; being Faroese coming to Denmark as an international student, those feel like particularly sensitive areas. An opt-out is good, but complete transparency about data security and usage would be even better. It's crucial this feels supportive, not punitive.

Thanks everyone – it’s really valuable to hear such honest reflections, especially from those with direct experience navigating difficulties. I definitely agree Q3 was tricky; quantifying ‘improvement’ feels detached and a bit… disrespectful, frankly, when we're talking about people struggling.

For me, explainability (Q4) is vital *because* of my own past dropout. If a model had flagged me, I’d want to understand *why*, not just be told “the system said so.” It feels empowering to know the reasoning. 

I was stricter on sensitive data – nationality, financial aid – because those feel like things that could easily reinforce existing inequalities. An opt-out is good, but transparency and robust security are crucial; it’s about building trust and making sure this actually *helps* students, not just categorizes them.

Thanks everyone for sharing – those were really insightful points, especially hearing directly from students about their concerns. I agree wholeheartedly with the difficulty of Q3; quantifying ‘improvement’ feels… reductive when we're talking about supporting individuals. As an advisor, I see so much nuance that a number can’t capture.

I think explainability (Q4) is absolutely critical – it impacts my ability to *actually* help students. While fairness (Q5) and robust data security are vital, I lean towards ‘moderate’ on Absalon data (Q3.4). Patterns of engagement *can* be early indicators if viewed alongside other factors. The opt-out suggestion is excellent; transparency is key, and a clear appeals process would go a long way in building trust with students.
